titleEn: Guanxi: why a favour in China is a long-term account
facts: Guanxi describes durable personal connections built through repeated exchanges of favours, information and introductions rather than through a contract or a job title.
The relationship is maintained by small reciprocal acts - a banquet, a hospital introduction, a lift for a child's school application - each of which creates a remembered obligation.
It is tied to face: declining a reasonable request can embarrass both sides, so refusals are softened, postponed or routed through an intermediary.

Scholars distinguish guanxi from ordinary networking because it is diffuse and long-term: the debt is not settled after one transaction but carried across years and sometimes into the next generation.
Business schools now teach guanxi as a form of social capital, while younger urban workers often describe it as expensive and tiring.
exampleEn: A project manager asks an old classmate to introduce a reliable supplier; months later the classmate calls in the favour when his nephew needs an internship.
qualificationEn: Guanxi is strong in business and state-linked circles but not universal; many urban and younger Chinese prefer formal contracts, and practices vary by region and generation.

titleEn: Why a Chinese child calls the neighbour Auntie and the shopkeeper Uncle
facts: Chinese address terms map age, generation and relationship rather than names: ayi (auntie) and shushu (uncle) are used for unrelated adults of the parents' generation.
The system distinguishes the father's side from the mother's (yeye versus waigong for grandfathers) and older from younger siblings, so a single English aunt covers several different words.
For strangers a surname plus a title is common - Wang laoshi (Teacher Wang) or Li shifu (Master Li) - and a bare personal name can sound abrupt.
These terms are not only labels: choosing the right one signals that the speaker understands the relationship and its obligations.
The same vocabulary travels with Chinese communities to Singapore, Malaysia and Taiwan, where local usage mixes with Malay, English and Hokkien conventions.
exampleEn: A child is told to greet a woman at the door as ayi; she is not a relative, but the term places her in the mother's generation, so the greeting comes with expected warmth.
qualificationEn: Terms differ across regions and families, and urban Chinese increasingly use given names or English names among peers; overseas communities adapt the system to local languages.

expression.glossEn: auntie - a courtesy term for a woman of one's parents' generation

titleEn: Chengyu: four characters that carry a whole classical story
facts: Chengyu are fixed four-character expressions, most distilled from classical histories, poems or philosophical texts, whose literal words rarely give the whole meaning.
Thousands remain in active use, and a well-placed chengyu signals education and wit in speech, essays and headlines.
Huà shé tiān zú (draw a snake and add feet) warns against ruining a good thing by overdoing it; shou zhu dai tu (guard the stump for a hare) mocks waiting for luck instead of working.
Because meaning depends on the underlying story, learners often memorise the anecdote along with the phrase.
Modern media and advertising play with chengyu by swapping one character, a pun that assumes the reader knows the original.
exampleEn: A colleague who keeps adding slides to a finished proposal may be told he is huà shé tiān zú - adding feet to the snake.
qualificationEn: Usage is uneven: some chengyu are literary and formal, others are common in speech, and many have variants or meanings that shifted from their classical sources.

expression.glossEn: to draw a snake and add feet - to ruin something by overdoing it

titleEn: Red envelopes: money that is given, refused and then accepted
facts: Hongbao are red paper packets filled with money, given at Lunar New Year, weddings and birthdays, with the red colour standing for luck and protection.
Etiquette can require the receiver to decline once or twice before accepting, and the giver may have to press the packet into a hand or pocket.
Amounts are chosen symbolically: even numbers are preferred, eight is lucky, and four is avoided because it sounds like death.
Since 2014 WeChat digital red packets have moved the custom into group chats, where split-second races to grab envelopes have become a New Year ritual.
The gift creates obligation and rank: who gives, how much and who receives are read as statements about status and closeness.
exampleEn: At a New Year dinner an uncle hands a child a hongbao; the parents say no, no before letting the child keep it, and the uncle later receives a return gift at another household.
qualificationEn: Amounts and etiquette vary by region, income and relationship; some families now cap red packets to avoid comparison, and digital envelopes have loosened old rules.

titleEn: Chunyun: the largest annual migration on earth
facts: Chunyun is the 40-day travel period around Lunar New Year, when students and migrant workers return home; it is often called the world's largest annual human migration.
Hundreds of millions of journeys are made by train, bus, plane and motorbike, and tickets for popular routes sell out within seconds on the 12306 booking system.
The rush exposes the split between registered hometowns and cities of work: many migrants can see parents and children only once a year.
Pandemic controls and official advice to stay put interrupted the pattern from 2020, and some cities now pay workers to celebrate locally.
Reverse travel - parents flying to the city instead of children going home - has grown as a quieter alternative.
exampleEn: A factory worker in Guangdong queues online for a hard-seat ticket to Sichuan, then spends 20 hours on a train to reach a village where his parents have kept his childhood room.
qualificationEn: The scale and dates vary year to year and were significantly disrupted by COVID-19 controls; not every family travels, and many urban-born Chinese stay in the city.

titleEn: Gaokao: three days that can decide a family's next decade
facts: The gaokao is the national university entrance examination, held in June; in recent years more than ten million candidates have sat it annually.
Scores are paired with provincial quotas and a ranked volunteer system, so a student's chance of a top university depends heavily on where the family is registered.
Households organise around the exam: quiet rooms, special meals, parents escorting children to the hall and police directing traffic near test centres.
The stakes have created a vast cram-school industry and heated debate about hukou inequality and exam stress.
Some provinces have introduced new subject-selection models, but the exam remains the main route into elite universities.
exampleEn: In a county high school the whole building is closed for revision week; a mother takes leave from work to cook, and a grandmother visits a temple for luck on the morning of the exam.
qualificationEn: Admission rules, subjects and competition differ by province and change frequently; vocational and overseas routes are growing alternatives, and not all families treat the exam as decisive.

titleEn: Meshrep: the Uyghur gathering that taught music, manners and community
facts: Meshrep is a community gathering among the Uyghurs of Xinjiang that combines music, dance, food, poetry and moral instruction; the word suggests a festive assembly.
It was traditionally held for weddings, harvests and neighbourhood events, with elders correcting behaviour and young people learning songs and manners.
UNESCO added the meshrep to its intangible cultural heritage list in 2010, describing it as a vehicle for transmitting social values.
Since 2017 many public meshrep events have been restricted under security policies in Xinjiang, and outside researchers have limited access to the region.
Uyghur diaspora communities in Central Asia and beyond hold meshrep as a way of maintaining language and identity.
exampleEn: A village wedding includes a meshrep in a courtyard: a dutar player leads songs, older men recite proverbs, and young guests are teased into dancing.
qualificationEn: Reporting on meshrep is contested: official Chinese sources emphasise cultural protection, while Uyghur and human-rights groups describe restrictions. Access to Xinjiang is tightly controlled, so details vary by source.

titleEn: Keigo: three layers of politeness inside one Japanese sentence
facts: Japanese honorific language (keigo) has three main registers: sonkeigo for elevating the listener, kenjōgo for humbling the speaker, and teineigo for general politeness.
The same action changes shape: iku (go) becomes mairimasu when humbling oneself and irasshaimasu when respecting the other person.
Business keigo is a second language for many recruits, who attend training and use manuals; errors are a common source of workplace embarrassment.
The system is entwined with uchi-soto: one speaks humbly about one's own group and respectfully about outsiders, so the same person may use different forms with a colleague and a client.
Younger speakers and service staff often use a simplified polite style, and linguists debate whether keigo is declining or simply changing.
exampleEn: A new employee answers the phone with osewa ni natte orimasu, then switches to humble forms when speaking about her own manager.
qualificationEn: Keigo is not a single fixed code: usage varies by region, company and generation, and over-formality can sound ironic or cold between close colleagues.

expression.original: お世話になっております
expression.glossEn: thank you for your continued support - the standard business greeting

titleEn: Aizuchi: the small noises that prove a Japanese listener is still there
facts: Aizuchi are the frequent interjections and nods - hai, ee, sō desu ne - that a listener makes while another person speaks.
They signal attention and participation rather than agreement, and Japanese speakers use them far more often than English speakers in comparable conversations.
The habit can mislead visitors: a Japanese listener saying yes, yes may be following the story, not consenting to a proposal.
Aizuchi are managed differently on the phone, where silence is more likely to be read as the line dropping.
Language teachers now explicitly teach both producing and interpreting aizuchi, since its absence can make a speaker seem cold or hostile.
exampleEn: On a video call a Tokyo manager keeps murmuring sō desu ne while a German supplier explains a delay; the supplier later learns the murmurs meant I am listening, not I agree.
qualificationEn: Frequency and form vary by region, age and gender, and video calls have changed the rhythm; overusing aizuchi with close friends can sound theatrical.

expression.glossEn: that's right, isn't it - a common listening backchannel

titleEn: Senpai and kōhai: how a graduation year organises Japanese daily life
facts: Senpai is someone who entered a school, club or company earlier; kōhai is the junior, and the pair shapes greetings, seating and speech.
The relationship is not merely rank: seniors are expected to mentor, protect and sometimes pay for juniors, while juniors use polite language and defer in decisions.
Sports clubs and university circles run on the distinction, with juniors cleaning, serving and addressing seniors by title rather than name.
In workplaces the pattern persists in training and after-hours socialising, though flat startup culture and remote work have weakened it.
The term has spread abroad through manga and anime, where senpai is often used as a form of address in translation communities.
exampleEn: A first-year member of a kyūdō club bows to the third-year students, carries their equipment and calls them senpai, and in return receives coaching and a place in the club's routines.
qualificationEn: The hierarchy is softer and more negotiated than the stereotype suggests; many clubs and companies now discourage rigid seniority, and age and length of service do not always align.

titleEn: Honne and tatemae: the difference between feeling and saying
facts: Honne is a person's true feeling or opinion; tatemae is the public stance adopted to keep a situation smooth.
The pair is not simply lying: tatemae is treated as a social form that protects the other person's face and keeps group harmony intact.
Context matters: honne is more freely expressed when drinking with close colleagues, among family or in private with friends.
The distinction appears in refusals, which may be phrased as it is a little difficult rather than a direct no, leaving the listener to infer the answer.
Foreign managers often misread tatemae as agreement, a gap that cross-cultural training programmes now address explicitly.
exampleEn: A supplier asks whether the deadline is possible; the manager says we will do our best (tatemae), then privately tells the team the date cannot be met (honne).
qualificationEn: The concept is an ideal type, not a rule: Japanese speakers vary widely in directness, and young people and international workplaces often mix both styles.

expression.glossEn: the public face or official stance presented to others

titleEn: Nemawashi: deciding the matter before the meeting starts
facts: Nemawashi means going around the roots: informal one-to-one conversations that build consent before a formal decision.
A proposal is discussed quietly with each affected person, objections are absorbed, and the meeting becomes a ratification rather than a debate.
The practice is often paired with ringi, the written approval system in which a document travels up the hierarchy collecting seals.
Nemawashi can make decisions slow to start but fast to implement, because resistance has already been addressed.
Remote work has strained the practice, since much of it happens in corridors, lunches and after-work conversations.
exampleEn: Before proposing a new workflow, a team leader visits four colleagues individually over a week; by the time the meeting is held, the change passes without argument.
qualificationEn: It is strongest in large traditional organisations and government; startups and foreign-owned firms often skip it, and critics say it can favour insiders and hide disagreement.

titleEn: Obon: the three days when the ancestors come home
facts: Obon is a Buddhist memorial period in mid-August in most of Japan - mid-July in some regions - when families welcome ancestral spirits back home.
Households clean graves, set offerings and light small welcome fires or lanterns; at the end, floating lanterns may be sent down rivers or to the sea.
Bon odori folk dances are held in neighbourhoods, often in a schoolyard or shrine grounds, and anyone can join the circle.
The holiday triggers one of Japan's biggest travel peaks as city dwellers return to ancestral towns.
Regional customs differ sharply: Okinawan Obon, for example, involves visits and songs that mainland families would not recognise.
exampleEn: A Tokyo family drives overnight to a mountain town, scrubs the grave, offers cucumbers and aubergines shaped like horses and cows, and joins the local bon odori in the evening.
qualificationEn: Dates, rites and the degree of religious observance vary by region, temple and family; many younger Japanese treat Obon mainly as a holiday for travel and family visits.

titleEn: Hanami: reading the week the cherries will open
facts: Hanami is the custom of viewing cherry blossoms in spring, usually with a picnic under the trees in parks, temple grounds and riverbanks.
Timing is everything: the Japan Meteorological Agency and private weather companies publish cherry-blossom forecasts, and the blossom front moves north through the islands.
The bloom lasts roughly one to two weeks depending on weather, so offices and friends track updates and book spots early.
The brevity of the blossom is a long-standing symbol in Japanese poetry and aesthetics, linked to mono no aware, an awareness of passing beauty.
Hanami is also a commercial season, with special sweets, beer and viewing cruises; some parks restrict alcohol after complaints about litter and noise.
exampleEn: Colleagues send a group-chat map of the bloom forecast, put down a blue plastic sheet at 8 a.m. to reserve a spot, and eat bento under the trees after work.
qualificationEn: Customs vary by region and climate, and the season can shift by two weeks; crowded urban parks have led some cities to ban early spot-reserving.

titleEn: Nomikai: the office dinner that does the work of a meeting
facts: A nomikai is an office drinking party, usually at an izakaya, held to welcome recruits, mark project endings or bond teams.
Seating is often hierarchical, glasses are refilled by others before one's own, and the most junior person may pour for seniors.
Alcohol is treated as a social permission slip: complaints that cannot be raised in the office may be aired after the second beer.
The obligatory feel has weakened: younger workers resist compulsory parties, and remote work and cost pressures have reduced their frequency.
The izakaya format - small dishes, all-you-can-drink plans, private rooms - grew to accommodate these group evenings.
exampleEn: After a product launch twenty colleagues sit in a private room; the youngest pours beer for the section chief, and the manager who has said little for weeks finally criticises the schedule.
qualificationEn: Not everyone drinks, and many companies now offer non-alcoholic options and daytime versions; the practice is less compulsory than the stereotype implies.

titleEn: Rakugo: one storyteller, one cushion, two characters
facts: Rakugo is a solo comic storytelling art in which a performer sits on a cushion, using a folding fan and a small cloth as the only props.
The teller plays all characters, switching voice, posture and gaze; the classical repertoire includes hundreds of stories, many ending in a pun called the ochi.
Most rakugo stories are set in the Edo period, and their humour depends on detailed knowledge of that world's shops, dialects and social types.
Training is apprenticeship-based and hierarchical, with performers taking stage names from their masters in a lineage.
Rakugo has been translated and performed in English, and a small international circuit now performs both classical and new material.
exampleEn: At a yose theatre in Tokyo the performer kneels, snaps open a fan to become a merchant, tilts his head to become the customer, and ends with a pun that makes the audience groan and clap.
qualificationEn: The art is not frozen: new material, dialect performances and overseas tours exist, and regional styles differ from the Tokyo mainstream.

titleEn: Manzai: the comedy double act built on speed and contradiction
facts: Manzai is a two-person comedy form in which a boke (fool) says something absurd and a tsukkomi (straight man) corrects or scolds him, often with a slap.
It developed around Osaka and Kyoto, and Kansai's faster, more combative comedy style is still contrasted with Tokyo's slower delivery.
The form is a major route to television fame: the M-1 Grand Prix, an annual contest for manzai duos, is a national event.
Most duos are freelance or agency-managed, and their material is polished live in small theatres before reaching TV.
Manzai's rhythm has influenced anime dubbing, variety shows and political satire, and it now tours international comedy festivals.
exampleEn: In an Osaka theatre the boke claims he can fly; the tsukkomi asks how, gets a confident absurd answer, and slaps him while the audience laughs at the timing.
qualificationEn: Osaka's style is not the only one, and modern duos blend manzai with sketch and stand-up; the slap is a convention, not literally violent intent.

titleEn: Korean speech levels: how one sentence changes with the listener
facts: Korean verbs carry endings that mark politeness and formality; the main contemporary levels are formal polite (-hamnida), informal polite (-haeyo) and casual or plain (-hae).
Choosing a level depends on age, rank, closeness and setting, and getting it wrong can sound rude or oddly distant.
The honorific infix -si- is added when the subject is someone to be respected, while humble verbs are used for oneself in some contexts.
Age matters so much that Koreans often ask a new acquaintance's age to know which level to use.
Speech levels are loosening online and among younger speakers, but workplace and family hierarchies still enforce them.
exampleEn: A junior employee says sugo hasyeotseumnida (you have worked hard) to a senior leaving the office, and switches to casual speech only with close same-age friends.
qualificationEn: Usage differs by region, generation and media; many Koreans mix levels within a conversation, and the North Korean system has diverged in vocabulary and norms.

expression.glossEn: you have worked hard - a polite acknowledgment to a colleague or senior

titleEn: Nunchi: the social skill of reading a room without being told
facts: Nunchi literally means eye measure, the ability to read another person's mood and the atmosphere of a situation quickly.
It is praised as a social virtue: a person with nunchi notices when a guest is uncomfortable, when a boss is angry or when it is time to leave.
The phrase nunchi eopda (to have no nunchi) is an insult, implying someone is oblivious to others.
Nunchi operates strongly in hierarchical settings, where direct disagreement is avoided and meaning must be inferred from tone and context.
Foreign residents often find it both a gift and a burden, since its absence can mark them as outsiders while its constant use is exhausting.
exampleEn: At a company dinner a new hire notices the team leader checking the time and quietly signals the group that the evening should end - no one has said anything.
qualificationEn: The concept idealises sensitivity but can also enable gossip and pressure to conform; younger Koreans increasingly value directness, and behaviour varies by context.

expression.glossEn: eye measure - the ability to read a situation and others' moods

titleEn: Kimjang: making kimchi together as a seasonal obligation
facts: Kimjang is the late-autumn practice of making large batches of kimchi to last through winter, usually as a family or neighbourhood event.
Cabbage is salted, rinsed and seasoned with chilli, garlic, ginger and fish sauce, then packed into jars or onggi pots and left to ferment.
The work is communal: relatives and neighbours gather to wash, season and pack, and the day ends with a shared meal of pork and fresh kimchi.
UNESCO recognised kimjang as intangible cultural heritage in 2013, citing the sharing of knowledge and the cooperative labour.
Apartment living and kimchi refrigerators have shrunk the ritual, and many urban families now buy kimchi or make a symbolic batch.
exampleEn: In November a family spreads tarpaulins in a courtyard, children carry salted cabbage, grandmothers judge the seasoning, and neighbours exchange jars the next morning.
qualificationEn: Recipes and timing vary by region and family, and commercial kimchi is now dominant; the communal version persists mainly among older and rural households.

titleEn: Seollal: bows, rice-cake soup and a family ledger
facts: Seollal is the Korean Lunar New Year, one of the year's two biggest holidays, when families gather in the ancestral hometown.
Younger people perform sebae, a deep bow to elders, and receive a greeting and often money; everyone eats tteokguk, a rice-cake soup that marks a year of age.
Families hold jesa rites for ancestors before the meal, setting out food in a prescribed arrangement and bowing in order of seniority.
Travel congestion is severe, and gift sets - fruit, meat and health products - are exchanged as tokens of respect.
The holiday is under pressure from small families, distance and the cost of gifts, and some couples now split the day between two households.
exampleEn: On New Year's morning a Seoul family sets the ancestral table, bows in turn, then the grandmother hands envelopes of money to the children before everyone sits down to tteokguk.
qualificationEn: Regional and family customs differ, and the ancestral rite is less common among Christians and younger urban households; dates follow the lunar calendar and shift each year.

titleEn: Jesa: setting a table for ancestors who are no longer there
facts: Jesa is a Korean ancestral rite held on the anniversary of a death, at Lunar New Year and at Chuseok.
The table is laid in a strict order of rows and positions, with fruit, rice, soup, meat and rice cakes placed according to rules that vary by family and region.
The head of the household leads the bows, pours liquor and recites, and the family shares the food afterwards, a practice called eumbok.
Jesa reflects Confucian ideas of filial duty and patrilineal continuity, and traditionally passed the role of chief mourner to the eldest son.
Participation has declined with smaller families and Christian affiliation, and some families simplify the rite or move it to a memorial park.
exampleEn: On the anniversary of his father's death a son sets a low table before dawn, pours rice wine three times, bows with his family, and then the group eats the offerings.
qualificationEn: Rituals vary widely by region, religion and family; Christian Koreans usually do not hold jesa, and many urban families have replaced it with quiet memorial visits.

titleEn: Arirang: a folk song that everyone sings a different way
facts: Arirang is a Korean folk song with many regional versions, all sharing the refrain Arirang and a tone of parting and longing.
The refrain is often sung as a call-and-response, and verses are improvised or composed locally, so the song exists in hundreds of variants.
It was used in the independence movement and later by both Koreas as a symbol of shared nationhood; UNESCO listed two versions in 2012.
Performers range from farmers' bands to symphony orchestras, and the song also became a standard in Korean diaspora communities.
In North Korea the name was given to a mass gymnastics festival, showing how one song can be claimed by rival political cultures.
exampleEn: At a rural funeral and at a concert hall the same melody is played at very different tempos; audiences often join the refrain without needing a lyric sheet.
qualificationEn: There is no single authorised version: melodies, lyrics and performance settings differ by region and era, and the two Koreas use the song in different political contexts.

titleEn: Suneung: the exam morning when the country makes way
facts: The suneung is the College Scholastic Ability Test, held on a Thursday in November and used by universities across South Korea.
On exam day offices open later to clear traffic, flights are held during the English listening section, and police escort late students to testing halls.
Families and churches hold prayer vigils, and younger students cheer the test-takers at the gates.
Competition for top universities feeds a large private academy industry and long study hours.
The exam's weight has been debated for years, and reforms have added comprehensive admissions and essay-based routes, but it still dominates the calendar.
exampleEn: On the morning of the test a mother hands her daughter a sticky rice cake, believing the stickiness will make the knowledge stick, while police motorcycles clear the road to the testing hall.
qualificationEn: Schedules and rules change with policy; not all students take the same route, and the influence of the exam is often exaggerated in foreign coverage.

titleEn: Taiwanese Hokkien: a mother tongue lost within a generation
facts: Taiwanese Hokkien was the everyday language of most families in Taiwan before 1945 and remains the ancestral language of a majority of the population.
After the Kuomintang arrived in 1949, Mandarin was promoted as the national language; school rules punished pupils for speaking Hokkien and television long favoured Mandarin.
The result is widespread passive understanding but declining active fluency, especially among younger urban Taiwanese.
Local-language education was reintroduced from the 1990s, and Hokkien now appears in campaigns, pop music and subtitles.
The language has no single standard writing system, so texts mix Chinese characters, romanisation and invented characters, which complicates teaching.
exampleEn: A grandmother asks a child chia̍h pá--bē (have you eaten?) as a greeting; the child understands but answers in Mandarin, and the grandmother repeats the question in Hokkien.
qualificationEn: Fluency varies sharply by region, generation and family; Hakka and Indigenous languages have their own revival movements, and Mandarin remains dominant in public life.

expression.glossEn: have you eaten yet? - a common everyday greeting

titleEn: Taiwan's night markets: the street as the family dining room
facts: Night markets are evening street-food districts found in most Taiwanese cities, with stalls selling snacks, drinks and small goods until late.
They grew from temple fairs and evening markets, and many are still anchored near a temple, where the crowd moves from worship to dinner.
Stalls specialise: one sells only oyster omelettes, another only shaved ice, and reputations spread by word of mouth and food blogs.
Families treat the market as a dining room: children do homework on folding tables, grandparents sit with tea, and office workers grab dinner on the way home.
Tourism and hygiene regulation have changed the markets, with some famous ones moving indoors or pedestrianising surrounding streets.
exampleEn: On a Friday night a family walks the same route: a bowl of noodles at one stall, fried chicken at another, then shaved ice shared at a corner table while scooters edge past.
qualificationEn: Markets differ greatly in size and authenticity; tourist-oriented ones raise prices, and summer heat and food-safety concerns shape what visitors choose.

titleEn: Kowloon Walled City: the densest place people ever called home
facts: The Kowloon Walled City was a 2.6-hectare enclave in Hong Kong that grew into a dense mass of unplanned buildings, home to an estimated 33,000 people at its peak.
It began as a Qing fort, became a Chinese exclave that British Hong Kong did not administer, and filled with squatters, workshops and clinics.
Inside, narrow stairways and rooftops formed a maze; dentists, noodle factories and unlicensed doctors operated in spaces that official maps barely recorded.
Britain and China agreed to demolish it in 1987, and the site was cleared between 1993 and 1994; a park now occupies the location.
The walled city has become a global reference for dense informal urbanism, studied by architects and cited in films and games.
exampleEn: Residents describe climbing unlit stairs to a rooftop where children flew kites, while below a dentist's chair sat in a room with no natural light.
qualificationEn: Population and living-condition figures are estimates from journalists and surveys, and the enclave was not typical of Hong Kong housing; its mythology often outruns the evidence.

titleEn: Macanese: a creole community built between empires
facts: The Macanese are a Eurasian community descended from Portuguese settlers, Chinese and South Asian merchants and enslaved people who lived in Macau over four centuries.
They developed a distinctive creole language, Patuá, and a cuisine that mixes Portuguese, Chinese, Indian and Malay ingredients.
Under Portuguese administration the community held a middle position in colonial society, and after the 1999 handover to China many emigrated to Portugal, Australia and Canada.
Macanese identity is now maintained through family networks, food festivals and heritage associations rather than everyday use of Patuá, which is critically endangered.
The community illustrates how port cities produce hybrid cultures that outlive the empires that made them.
exampleEn: A Macanese family in Lisbon cooks minchi and capela on Sundays, speaks Portuguese at home and trades Patuá phrases with relatives in Macau over video calls.
qualificationEn: The community is small and internally varied, and Macanese can mean different things in Macau, Portugal and the diaspora; the creole language has very few fluent speakers.

titleEn: Naadam: three sports, one national holiday
facts: Naadam is Mongolia's national festival, held in mid-July, built around the three manly games of wrestling, horse racing and archery.
Wrestlers compete without weight classes; horse races are run across open steppe by child jockeys, and archery targets are shot in teams.
The festival opens with elaborate ceremonies in Ulaanbaatar and is celebrated in provincial towns and herding settlements with local competitions.
UNESCO listed the Naadam festival as intangible cultural heritage in 2010, noting its role in transmitting nomadic skills and social values.
Naadam is also a family reunion and trading occasion, with food stalls, concerts and visitors returning from the capital.
exampleEn: In a provincial Naadam a child jockey rides a horse for 15 kilometres, wrestlers in studded boots dance into the ring, and families set up felt tents around the edge of the field.
qualificationEn: Rules and scales vary by province, and urban Naadam is partly a state spectacle; horse-race distances and child-jockey safety are subjects of ongoing reform.

titleEn: Namaste: a greeting that measures respect
facts: Namaste is a greeting made with palms pressed together at the chest, sometimes with a slight bow, used across Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh communities in South Asia.
The word comes from Sanskrit and is often glossed as I bow to you, acknowledging a shared inner self rather than physical contact.
It works for both hello and goodbye and avoids the handshake problem of unequal status and ritual purity.
A younger person usually greets an elder first, and a more elaborate form such as namaskar or a deeper bow signals greater respect.
The gesture has travelled globally through yoga and diaspora practice, often with its religious meaning flattened into a wellness signal.
exampleEn: A student enters a classroom in Varanasi, presses her palms together and says namaste to the teacher before sitting; the teacher returns it with a small nod.
qualificationEn: Forms differ by region and religion, and urban Indians increasingly mix namaste with handshakes or hugs; the gesture's meaning changes in yoga studios outside South Asia.

expression.glossEn: I bow to you - hello and goodbye

titleEn: Jugaad: the improvisation people admire and sometimes resent
facts: Jugaad describes a frugal, improvised solution - a workaround made from what is at hand - and is a widely used Hindi term in Indian English.
The classic image is a homemade vehicle cobbled together from a water pump and a motorcycle, but the word covers everything from repaired appliances to informal transport.
It is celebrated as resourcefulness in business schools and startup culture, where frugal innovation is a close cousin.
Critics note the flip side: jugaad can mean cutting corners on safety, quality or paperwork, and the word can hint at someone who bends rules.
Foreign companies operating in India often must learn to work with it rather than against it, since informal solutions fill gaps in services.
exampleEn: When the office internet fails before a deadline a clerk tethers his phone, borrows a laptop charger from a neighbour and sends the file from the rooftop where the signal is strong.
qualificationEn: The concept is romanticised in popular media; its quality ranges from genuine engineering to unsafe improvisation, and usage varies across regions and classes.

titleEn: Dabbawalas: 130 years of lunch delivery without an app
facts: Mumbai's dabbawalas collect home-cooked lunches from suburban homes and deliver them to office workers across the city, then return the empty boxes.
They handle roughly 200,000 boxes a day with a hand-written colour-and-symbol code, and no barcodes or smartphones in the core sorting.
The service began in the 1890s and is organised as a cooperative of small teams, each owning the rights to certain routes and customers.
Error rates are famously low - a Six Sigma study in 2001 found about one mistake per six million transactions, though the claim is often repeated uncritically.
The system survived the growth of food delivery apps by relying on trust and very low cost, though COVID-19 briefly halved demand.
exampleEn: A home cook packs two tiffin boxes, a runner picks them up at the station, sorters match the colour code to a building, and the office worker finds hot lunch on her desk at 12:30.
qualificationEn: The service is concentrated in Mumbai and has been disrupted by remote work and food apps; the Six Sigma error figure is often quoted more precisely than the evidence supports.

titleEn: Langar: the free kitchen where everyone sits on the floor
facts: Langar is the community kitchen in Sikh gurdwaras, where free meals are served to anyone regardless of religion, caste, gender or wealth.
The meal is usually simple - dal, rice, bread, vegetables and kheer - cooked and served by volunteers, and diners sit together on the floor in rows called pangat.
The practice expresses two core Sikh ideas: equality and seva, or selfless service; the Golden Temple in Amritsar serves tens of thousands of meals daily.
Running a gurdwara's langar is a major voluntary operation: devotees donate ingredients, wash dishes and clean up, and roles rotate.
Langar travels with the diaspora, and Sikh communities in Britain, Canada and the United States are known for feeding frontline workers and the homeless.
exampleEn: On a Sunday in Amritsar a volunteer ladles dal into steel bowls while a businessman and a labourer sit shoulder to shoulder on the floor, and everyone is served before the next batch.
qualificationEn: Practices vary by gurdwara and tradition, and some larger sites now use industrial equipment; the meal is not charity aimed at outsiders but an expression of the community's own principles.

titleEn: Hinglish: the code-switch that runs Indian cities
facts: Hinglish is the mixed Hindi-English speech common in urban India, where sentences switch languages mid-clause and English words take Hindi verb endings.
It has colonial roots but became a mass register through films, advertising and the internet, especially among young urban speakers.
It signals class, education and informality at once: a Hindi sentence with English technical nouns can sound modern, while heavy Hinglish in a formal setting can sound crude.
The vocabulary has spread into Indian English - prepone for moving a meeting earlier, timepass for idle distraction - words that mark South Asian usage.
Writers and advertisers use Hinglish to sound authentic, and linguists study it as an example of code-switching as a stable social practice rather than a failure of bilingualism.
exampleEn: A colleague says meeting prepone kar diya hai, 11 baje aa jao, mixing English nouns with Hindi grammar; everyone understands without changing register.
qualificationEn: Hinglish is not one uniform language: its mix varies by region, class, generation and medium, and large parts of India use other language mixtures or neither Hindi nor English.

expression.glossEn: okay, I see - a common conversational acknowledgment

titleEn: Caste: how heredity still shapes the everyday
facts: Caste in India combines varna, a classical four-part schema, with jati, thousands of local hereditary groups that regulate marriage, occupation and ritual status.
Jati endogamy - marrying within one's group - is the practice that has most persisted across urban and rural life.
India's constitution abolished untouchability and created reserved places in education, jobs and legislatures for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, with Other Backward Classes added later.
Discrimination based on caste is illegal, but studies and news reports document continued barriers in housing, marriage and workplace networks.
Caste interacts with class and religion, and it varies regionally: its forms in Kerala, Punjab and Bihar differ substantially.
exampleEn: A family advertises for a bride within our community, and a matrimonial website offers a compulsory caste filter, even in cities where colleagues share lunch without asking.
qualificationEn: Caste is not a single uniform hierarchy and has changed greatly with urbanisation, education and law; generalisations from one region can mislead, and caste among Sikhs, Christians and Muslims takes different forms.

titleEn: The Hindu joint family: a household with many centres of authority
facts: A Hindu joint family is a multi-generation household, traditionally patrilineal and patrilocal, in which sons bring wives into the parental home and property is shared.
Authority usually sits with the eldest male, while the eldest woman manages the kitchen and household labour; daughters move to their husband's family.
The household is also a ritual and economic unit: it maintains the family shrine, funds weddings and cares for elderly members.
Urban migration, smaller families and women's employment have increased nuclear households, but joint families persist in business communities and in care arrangements.
Jointness can be a resource - shared childcare, pooled savings - and a constraint, with limited privacy and unequal domestic labour.
exampleEn: In a family home three generations share a kitchen schedule; the grandmother supervises cooking, one son manages the family shop, and a daughter-in-law negotiates when to visit her own parents.
qualificationEn: The joint family is an ideal type, not a universal living arrangement; practice varies by region, caste, religion and class, and many households are nuclear or split across cities.

titleEn: Garba: Navaratri's all-night circle dance
facts: Garba is a Gujarati folk dance performed in a circle around a decorated lamp or image of the goddess, especially during the nine nights of Navaratri.
Dancers move in steps that alternate claps and turns; traditionally the dance is performed by women and girls, with men joining dandiya raas nearby.
The word garba refers to the earthen lamp placed at the centre, and the dance enacts devotion and community rather than a performance for an audience.
In Gujarat, neighbourhood garba grounds draw thousands of dancers; in cities abroad, community groups hire halls and keep the all-night format.
UNESCO added Garba of Gujarat to its intangible heritage list in 2023, noting its inclusive, participatory character.
exampleEn: On the third night of Navaratri a courtyard fills with women in mirror-work skirts; the circle expands as neighbours join, and the songs run until dawn.
qualificationEn: Styles and songs vary by region and community, and large commercial events have changed the atmosphere; the all-night format is not universal, and some families keep quieter domestic observances.

titleEn: UPI: paying the vegetable seller with a QR code
facts: The Unified Payments Interface is India's instant bank-to-bank payment system, launched in 2016 and now processing billions of transactions a month.
It works through a phone app, a virtual address and increasingly a QR code stuck to a stall, so street vendors, auto-rickshaw drivers and temples accept digital payment.
The system is interoperable across banks and apps, which helped it spread faster than single-company wallets.
UPI has changed everyday life - splitting bills, paying domestic workers, sending money home - but feature-phone users and poor connectivity remain excluded.
It is also a state-backed infrastructure that other countries study as an alternative to card networks.
exampleEn: At a roadside stall a customer scans a laminated QR code, pays twenty rupees and shows the green tick, while the seller's voice speaker announces the amount in Hindi.
qualificationEn: Digital payment is widespread but not universal, and fraud, privacy and rural connectivity are real concerns; adoption varies by state, age and income.

titleEn: The monsoon: a season that sets the household calendar
facts: The South Asian monsoon arrives in June and withdraws by September, delivering most of the region's annual rainfall and shaping agriculture, festivals and prices.
The India Meteorological Department publishes forecasts and a daily progression map; farmers wait for the first rains to sow, and weddings often wait for the dry months after.
Monsoon failure or delay can raise food prices and rural distress, while intense spells cause floods in cities such as Mumbai.
The season is celebrated in poetry, music and festivals, and the smell of the first rain is a common cultural image.
Climate change is making the monsoon more variable, with longer dry spells and heavier downpours.
exampleEn: In late June a family watches the sky, the first heavy rain drums on the roof, children run outside to get wet, and the grandmother starts planning the sowing.
qualificationEn: Rainfall timing and intensity vary greatly across India and South Asia; the monsoon is not a single uniform season, and regional cultures attach different meanings to it.

titleEn: Pashtunwali: an unwritten code of hospitality, honour and refuge
facts: Pashtunwali is the customary code of the Pashtun people, built around melmastia (hospitality), nanawatai (offering refuge) and badal (reciprocity or revenge).
Hospitality obliges a household to shelter and feed any guest for three days, regardless of cost or the guest's identity.
Nanawatai allows a person to ask for protection even from an enemy; granting it places the host's honour on the line.
The code is enforced through jirgas, councils of elders that settle disputes by consensus and customary precedent rather than state courts.
Pashtunwali is not a written law and varies by tribe and region; it coexists uneasily with modern legal systems in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
exampleEn: A stranger fleeing a dispute knocks on a village door and asks for nanawatai; the host shelters him first and only afterwards asks what happened, because protection comes before explanation.
qualificationEn: The code is an ideal invoked in disputes, not a script followed uniformly; tribal practice differs, and many Pashtuns live urban lives in which state law and Islam are more decisive.

titleEn: Basant: the spring sky full of fighting kites
facts: Basant is a spring festival in Punjab, historically associated with kite flying in Lahore and other cities as the weather warms in February.
Kite fighters cut rivals' lines with glass-coated string called manja, and rooftops fill with families and music; the sport is called kite fighting.
The festival has Hindu roots and was adopted across communities; in Pakistan it became a popular urban celebration and a tourist draw.
Safety concerns about metal-coated and glass-coated string led to bans and restricted seasons, and enforcement has varied by province and government.
Basant also exists in Indian Punjab and among the diaspora, where it is often a cultural rather than religious occasion.
exampleEn: In February a Lahore rooftop fills with cousins holding spool reels; a kite duel draws shouts when a string cuts, and the winner's kite drifts over the neighbourhood.
qualificationEn: Bans, dates and enthusiasm vary by city and year; the festival is celebrated by Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs in different ways, and official restrictions have pushed much flying underground.

titleEn: Qawwali: turning a shrine courtyard into a trance floor
facts: Qawwali is a devotional music form of South Asian Sufism, performed by a lead singer, a chorus, harmonium, tabla and dholak.
Songs set Urdu and Punjabi mystical poetry to repeated refrains that build intensity, and listeners may enter a state of spiritual absorption.
It grew in the Chishti Sufi tradition, centred on shrines in what is now Pakistan and India, and is performed at urs commemorations and private mehfils.
Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan brought qawwali to global audiences in the 1980s and 1990s, and the form now appears in film soundtracks and fusion projects.
Performers often improvise verses and change tempo in response to the audience, making each performance different.
exampleEn: At a shrine courtyard in Lahore the lead singer repeats a line and raises his hand; the harmonium swells, listeners stand and sway, and the crowd presses closer to the stage.
qualificationEn: Qawwali is devotional practice, not only concert music, and its lyrics come from several languages and poetic traditions; trance is not guaranteed or required.

titleEn: Adda: the purposeless conversation that holds Bengali life together
facts: Adda is the Bengali practice of long, informal conversation - at a tea stall, a bookshop, a street corner or someone's sitting room - with no agenda and no need to conclude.
The talk ranges from politics and cricket to gossip and philosophy, and the pleasure lies in the exchange rather than a decision.
Adda was central to colonial-era Bengali intellectual life, and coffee houses and bookshops in Kolkata became famous venues for it.
In Dhaka and Kolkata, older adda culture is often described as retreating before smartphones, commuting and smaller apartments.
The practice has literary status: essayists and filmmakers have treated adda as a distinctly Bengali social form.
exampleEn: Three friends meet at a tea stall after work, order endless small glasses of tea, argue about a film for two hours and go home without deciding anything.
qualificationEn: Adda is more of an ideal than a uniform institution, and its forms differ between Bangladesh and West Bengal; not everyone has the leisure or space for it.

titleEn: Pohela Boishakh: a new year that became a civic procession
facts: Pohela Boishakh is the Bengali New Year, celebrated on 14 April in Bangladesh and 15 April in parts of India, following the revised Bengali calendar.
In Dhaka the day opens with the Mangal Shobhajatra, a mass procession of huge masks and motifs organised by art students, which UNESCO listed as intangible heritage in 2016.
Businesses open new account books in a ritual called halkhata, and families eat panta bhat with fried fish, a simple dish associated with the day.
The festival was promoted in the 1960s as a secular Bengali identity marker distinct from religious holidays.
Celebrations include fairs, songs and red-and-white clothing, and have spread to Bengali communities abroad.
exampleEn: Before sunrise students lift a giant tiger-and-bird mask onto bamboo frames, drummers tune up, and the procession winds through Dhaka while families wear red and white and visit fairs.
qualificationEn: Dates and customs differ between Bangladesh, West Bengal and Tripura, and the festival mixes secular and religious elements; the Mangal Shobhajatra began only in 1989.

titleEn: The language movement: when a script became a country's reason
facts: After Partition in 1947, Pakistan's government promoted Urdu as the sole state language, though a majority of East Pakistan's population spoke Bengali.
Students and cultural organisations protested; on 21 February 1952 police fired on a demonstration in Dhaka, killing several students.
The deaths became a founding memory, and 21 February is now UNESCO's International Mother Language Day.
Bengali was recognised as a state language in 1956, and the movement helped build the political consciousness that led to Bangladesh's independence in 1971.
The Shaheed Minar monument in Dhaka marks the site, and the day is observed with barefoot processions and songs.
exampleEn: At midnight on 21 February crowds walk barefoot to the Shaheed Minar holding flowers, and schoolchildren sing the song Amar Bhaier Rokte Rangano (My brother's blood dyed it red).
qualificationEn: The movement's history is commemorated differently in Bangladesh and Pakistan, and language politics in the region also involved other languages such as Urdu, Sindhi and Punjabi.

titleEn: Esala Perahera: a procession of fire, elephants and caste duties
facts: The Esala Perahera is an annual Buddhist procession in Kandy, Sri Lanka, held in July or August and lasting about ten nights.
It escorts a casket believed to contain a relic of the Buddha from the Temple of the Tooth, with dancers, drummers, fire twirlers and decorated elephants.
The procession is organised by hereditary castes and temple tenants, each with specific duties; the diyawadana nilame, the lay custodian of the temple, leads arrangements.
The final Randoli Perahera is the grandest, and a water-cutting ceremony ends the festival at the Mahaweli River.
The event is both religious and a major tourist attraction, and elephant welfare has become a public debate.
exampleEn: On the last night caparisoned elephants walk under electric lights, Kandyan dancers leap to drumbeats, and fire twirlers spin flaming coconut shells along the route.
qualificationEn: Ritual details and caste roles vary by temple and region, and the Kandy event is not the only perahera; animal welfare concerns have led to restrictions on elephant participation.

titleEn: Chhaupadi: the menstrual exile that law has not ended
facts: Chhaupadi is a practice in parts of western Nepal in which menstruating women and girls are isolated in a shed or cattle stall, barred from the home and kitchen.
The custom is rooted in local beliefs about ritual purity, but it carries serious risks: cold, smoke, snake bites and sexual violence have caused deaths.
Nepal's Supreme Court banned the practice in 2005, and a 2017 law criminalised forcing someone to observe it, with fines and jail terms.
Enforcement remains weak in remote districts, and awareness campaigns, police and local governments have had uneven results.
The practice is not universal in Nepal and is strongest in the Far West and some Mid-Western districts.
exampleEn: A schoolgirl in a hill district is sent to a small mud shed during her period, misses classes for days, and returns to find her teacher has spoken to her parents.
qualificationEn: Reporting often generalises the practice to all of Nepal; it is a localised custom contested by many Nepalis, and precise prevalence estimates are difficult.

titleEn: Gross National Happiness: a national policy that measures the mind
facts: Bhutan's Gross National Happiness framework treats well-being, not GDP, as the goal of development; it was articulated by King Jigme Singye Wangchuck in the 1970s.
The 2008 constitution makes the state responsible for promoting GNH, and a GNH Commission screens policies against nine domains including health, education, culture and ecology.
Periodic national surveys produce a GNH index, used to classify citizens as deeply happy, extensively happy or unhappy.
Bhutan's policies - forest cover, tourism fees, tobacco restrictions - are often explained through GNH, though critics say the framework is also a branding tool.
The idea has been popularised internationally, with the UN adopting a resolution on happiness and well-being in 2011.
exampleEn: A road or school proposal in Thimphu must pass a GNH screening that asks how it affects community vitality and ecological resilience, not only its cost.
qualificationEn: GNH is a state framework, not a description of how every Bhutanese person feels; its indices and policy application are debated, and tourism and television have changed expectations.

titleEn: Dhivehi and Thaana: a script written right to left
facts: Dhivehi is the Indo-Aryan language of the Maldives, written in Thaana, a script that runs right to left and mixes Arabic-derived and Indian-derived letter forms.
Thaana developed in the sixteenth century, replacing an older script called Dhives Akuru, and its letters are named after Arabic numerals.
The language has heavy Arabic vocabulary for religion and administration, and Portuguese and English loanwords for trade and technology.
English is the medium of secondary and higher education, so many Maldivians switch languages daily between school, home and island work.
Dhivehi dialects differ across atolls, with the southernmost forms markedly distinct from the Male standard.
exampleEn: A teacher writes a note on the board in Thaana, reading right to left, then switches to English for the science lesson while students copy both.
qualificationEn: The standard is based on the Male dialect, and atoll varieties can be hard for outsiders to follow; English and Arabic dominate many formal and religious contexts.

titleEn: The wai: a Thai greeting that encodes rank
facts: A wai is made by pressing the palms together in front of the face or chest and bowing the head; the height of the hands and depth of the bow signal the relative status of the two people.
Thais generally wai first to elders, teachers, monks and superiors, while a junior may receive a shallower return wai.
The gesture is also used for apology, thanks and farewell, and its meaning depends on context and tone of voice.
Foreigners are usually not expected to initiate a wai, and an awkward wai can be more embarrassing than a handshake.
Monks, royalty and images of the Buddha receive specific forms of respect, and touching someone's head or pointing a foot remains rude.
exampleEn: A student wais a teacher with palms at the chin, receives a lower wai in return, and then walks past the school shrine with her hands still together.
qualificationEn: Practice varies by region, age and urbanisation, and many young Thais use a friendly nod with peers; the wai is not required in every encounter.

expression.glossEn: hello - usually said while making a wai

titleEn: Sanuk: why Thai social life is organised around having fun
facts: Sanuk means fun or enjoyment, and the word is used to describe work, eating, travel and even difficult tasks done in a pleasurable way.
The value shapes social expectations: a gathering that is too serious may be judged a failure, and humour is used to soften bad news and conflict.
Sanuk overlaps with the idea of mai pen rai (never mind), a relaxed response to setbacks that outsiders sometimes read as indifference.
Workplaces stage parties, sports days and offsite trips under the sanuk label, and Thai advertising leans heavily on humour.
The concept is an idealisation: long hours, traffic and family obligations mean not every day is fun, and critics say the pressure to be cheerful can suppress complaint.
exampleEn: A team finishing an exhausting inventory still orders food, plays music and turns the last hour into a game, because the group's mood matters as much as the deadline.
qualificationEn: Sanuk is a cultural keyword, not a description of every Thai person; age, class and region affect how much fun is expected, and tourist brochures exaggerate it.

titleEn: Songkran: the new year celebrated by throwing water
facts: Songkran is the Thai New Year, marked from 13 to 15 April, when families pour scented water over Buddha images and the hands of elders as a blessing.
The water ritual has expanded into public street water fights in cities such as Bangkok and Chiang Mai, drawing huge crowds of locals and tourists.
Traditionally water symbolises washing away the past year, and the pouring over elders is an act of respect, not play.
The festival is also a family holiday: many workers return to their home provinces, and temples hold special ceremonies and sand-stupa building.
Road safety during the travel period is a recurring concern, and authorities campaign against drink-driving each year.
exampleEn: On the first morning a family pours jasmine-scented water over the hands of grandparents, then children join the street where pickup trucks carry barrels of water and passers-by get soaked.
qualificationEn: The boisterous street version is only part of the festival, and observances differ by region and religion; some Thais keep the day quietly at home, and water fights have faced local restrictions.

titleEn: Tết: the new year that sends everyone home
facts: Tết is the Vietnamese Lunar New Year, the year's central family holiday, when people return to their home towns and villages.
Homes are cleaned, ancestral altars are set with fruit and flowers, and the first visitor of the year is chosen carefully because their character is believed to influence the household's luck.
Food is prepared days ahead: bánh chưng (square sticky-rice cakes), pickled onions, dried fruit and a tray of five fruits.
Children receive red envelopes called lì xì with money, and families visit graves and temples; the first days are reserved for relatives, later days for friends.
Traffic and travel demand peak before the holiday, and the government has extended holidays and encouraged road-safety campaigns.
exampleEn: A family in Ho Chi Minh City loads a motorbike with a peach branch and bánh chưng, rides 500 km to a Mekong village, and arrives in time to clean the ancestral altar before midnight.
qualificationEn: Customs vary between north and south Vietnam and among religious communities; urban families sometimes stay in the city, and travel chaos is part of the shared national story.

titleEn: Vietnamese pronouns: why I depends on who you are talking to
facts: Vietnamese pronouns are kinship terms: a speaker calls themselves em (younger sibling), anh (older brother) or chi (older sister) depending on the listener's age and relationship, not on gender alone.
The same person can be I in several ways in one day, and switching pronouns changes the emotional distance of a conversation.
Politeness particles such as a and da are added to show respect, especially to elders and in formal service settings.
Getting the age relationship wrong can cause offence, so Vietnamese often ask a new acquaintance's age or year of birth early.
Young urban speakers borrow English you and I in casual texting, and the internet has produced new address forms.
exampleEn: A shop assistant greets an older customer as anh or chi, calls herself em, and adds a polite particle at the end of sentences; with a friend of the same age she would switch to toi and ban.
qualificationEn: Usage varies by region, generation and setting, and the system is not rigid: speakers negotiate pronouns to change tone, and overseas Vietnamese adapt it to local languages.

expression.glossEn: polite particle used when answering an elder or showing deference

titleEn: Áo dài: the Vietnamese tunic that became a school uniform
facts: The áo dài is a close-fitting silk tunic with long side slits, worn over trousers by both women and men, and it is the best-known Vietnamese garment.
Its modern form was promoted in the 1930s and 1950s, and it became the uniform of many girls' secondary schools in South Vietnam and later across the country.
Wearing it is a mark of formality: teachers, flight attendants, brides and festival-goers wear versions in different colours and fabrics.
The dress is associated with grace and modesty, and its long slits allow movement while covering the body.
Debates recur about whether school uniforms should be mandatory, given cost and practicality, and designers keep modernising the cut.
exampleEn: At a high-school graduation in Hue, girls in white áo dài and boys in dark versions line up for photographs while teachers in silk versions supervise.
qualificationEn: Styles and rules differ by region, school and occasion, and many students wear uniforms only on special days; the dress is not everyday wear for most Vietnamese.

titleEn: Thanaka: the yellow paste that protects and decorates a Myanmar face
facts: Thanaka is a cosmetic paste made by grinding the bark of several trees on a flat stone with water; it is applied to the face and arms in Myanmar.
It is used for sun protection, cooling, skin care and decoration, and many women and children wear it daily, often in neat circles or leaf patterns.
Application is a social ritual: children learn to grind the bark, and a mother may prepare paste for the whole family in the morning.
The practice is centuries old and appears in Burmese art and poetry; a face streaked with thanaka is a common image of Myanmar in local media.
Modern cosmetics and urban lifestyles have reduced use among some young people, but it remains widespread and is sold in markets as cut logs and ready-made paste.
exampleEn: A girl in Mandalay grinds bark on a round stone with drops of water, spreads a yellow circle on each cheek before school, and carries the stone to the family's stall later.
qualificationEn: Use varies by region, age and class; men and boys use it less often, and some urban professionals wear it only at festivals or avoid it in office settings.

titleEn: Thingyan: the Burmese new year of water and merit
facts: Thingyan is the Burmese New Year festival, held in mid-April over several days, when water is thrown and poured to wash away the old year.
The ritual is linked to Buddhist merit-making: families bathe images of the Buddha, wash the hair of elders, and give food and alms to monks.
Cities set up pandals (stages) with hoses and music, and crowds douse passers-by; the holiday is also a time for feasts and the Burmese snack mont lone yay paw.
The new year begins after the water festival, and the first day is marked with silence and temple visits in many households.
Thingyan was suspended or restricted during the COVID-19 pandemic and under security restrictions after the 2021 coup, while many people continue private observances.
exampleEn: On the first day of Thingyan a family pours scented water over a small Buddha image, washes an elderly aunt's hair, then children join the street pandal where a hose soaks everyone.
qualificationEn: Observances differ between cities, villages and Buddhist communities; the street party image dominates foreign coverage, but the religious and family rites are central for many.

titleEn: Shinbyu: the ordination that turns a boy into a little monk
facts: Shinbyu is the Burmese ceremony in which boys, usually between seven and thirteen, are ordained as novice monks for a short period, often a week or a few months.
The ceremony is a major family event: the boy's head is shaved, he is dressed as a prince for a procession, and then he puts on the robe and receives alms.
It marks the family's Buddhist merit and is often held together with ear-piercing ceremonies for girls.
Monasteries depend on temporary novices, and the experience is meant to teach discipline, chanting and the Buddhist precepts.
In recent decades cost and social change have reduced the scale of some ceremonies, but shinbyu remains a common rite of passage.
exampleEn: A boy in a sequinned prince costume rides a cart through the village with drummers and relatives; at the monastery he changes into a robe, has his head shaved and receives his first alms bowl.
qualificationEn: Practices vary by region and family wealth, and not every boy is ordained; the length of stay and scale of celebration differ widely.

titleEn: Pchum Ben: feeding the ancestors for fifteen days
facts: Pchum Ben is a Cambodian Buddhist festival in the tenth lunar month, when families make offerings to deceased relatives over about fifteen days.
People bring rice, sweet cakes and fruit to pagodas, and monks chant; some families visit several temples to reach ancestors who may have moved on.
The belief is that the gates of the underworld open and hungry spirits search for offerings, so failing to make merit could leave relatives suffering.
The festival is one of the year's biggest travel periods, as people return to home provinces and family graves, and pagodas fill before dawn.
It combines Theravada Buddhist practice with pre-Buddhist ancestor beliefs, and it is also a social occasion for distant relatives to meet.
exampleEn: Before sunrise a family carries baskets of rice balls to a pagoda, offers them to monks and pours water on the ground for ancestors, then shares a meal with relatives they see once a year.
qualificationEn: Timing and local customs vary by commune and temple, and observance is not universal among Cambodians; urban families often give money or food rather than attend a full fortnight.

titleEn: The krama: one scarf, a hundred uses
facts: The krama is a woven cotton scarf, usually in a red-and-white or blue-and-white checked pattern, worn by Khmers in Cambodia.
It is used as a head covering, shoulder cloth, towel, basket, hammock for babies and padding for loads, which makes it more a tool than an accessory.
Different patterns and colours can indicate region, gender and occasion, and the krama has become a symbol of Cambodian identity.
During the Khmer Rouge years the krama was worn by cadre and also used to carry belongings during forced evacuations, giving it complex memories.
Today it is sold to tourists and worn by farmers, tuk-tuk drivers and officials alike, though cheaper imported scarves compete with hand-woven versions.
exampleEn: A tuk-tuk driver wraps a krama around his neck at dawn, uses a second one to shade a passenger, and ties a third to the frame to hold a spare tyre.
qualificationEn: Designs and uses vary by region and community, and the scarf's symbolism is not read the same way by everyone; the tourist version is often factory-made.

titleEn: Utang na loob: the debt that cannot be paid with money
facts: Utang na loob is a Filipino idea of a debt of gratitude owed to someone who helped in a time of need; the phrase means a debt of one's inner self.
It is not a financial obligation and is not settled by repayment; it is carried as a lasting bond and repaid through loyalty, service and future help.
The concept is central to family life: children are seen as owing their parents for life, and siblings and godparents are tied into webs of obligation.
It can be a source of mutual support and also a burden, as refusing a request from a benefactor is socially costly.
Filipino psychology treats utang na loob as one of several core values alongside pakikisama (getting along) and hiya (shame).
exampleEn: A woman who was helped through university by an aunt later gives that aunt's son a job, and the family treats this as repayment of a debt that was never financial.
qualificationEn: The concept is an ideal described in Filipino psychology, not a rule that everyone follows; urban and younger Filipinos negotiate it differently, and it can be exploited.

titleEn: Balikbayan boxes: migration packed into a cardboard box
facts: A balikbayan box is a cardboard cargo box sent home by overseas Filipinos, filled with clothes, food, toys and household goods for relatives.
The word balikbayan means returning to the country, and the box is a way for migrant workers to be present at home even when they cannot travel.
Boxes are collected by cargo companies, shipped in containers and delivered to provincial addresses; personal effects sent this way have a tax-free privilege.
Sending a box is a family ritual: relatives list what they need, the sender fills gaps, and the arrival is photographed and shared.
The practice reflects the scale of Filipino labour migration and the economy of remittances, which accounts for a large share of national income.
exampleEn: A Filipino nurse in Dubai packs a box with chocolate, shoes, shampoo and a tablet for her nephew, drops it at a cargo office eight weeks before Christmas, and tracks it as it lands in Cagayan de Oro.
qualificationEn: Customs rules and cargo companies vary, and not every migrant sends boxes; the practice is concentrated among workers who can afford shipping, and it is partly a middle-class family ritual.

titleEn: Mano po: asking an elder's hand for a blessing
facts: Mano po is a Filipino greeting in which a younger person takes an elder's right hand and presses it to their forehead, saying mano po.
The gesture asks for a blessing and shows respect; it is common when meeting grandparents, godparents and relatives at family gatherings.
It is related to Catholic practice, where the hand may be kissed or touched, and it is performed especially at holidays and family reunions.
The use is declining in some urban families, where a hug or a verbal greeting is preferred, but it persists in close family contexts.
The phrase combines mano (hand) and po, the Tagalog politeness particle, which also marks respect in speech generally.
exampleEn: On Christmas morning children queue to take their grandfather's hand, touch it to their foreheads and say mano po, and in return they receive a gift and a blessing.
qualificationEn: Practice varies by region, family and religion; some families use it only with very close elder relatives, and non-Filipinos are rarely expected to attempt it.

expression.glossEn: your hand, please - a greeting that asks an elder for a blessing

titleEn: Gotong royong: the village habit of doing things together
facts: Gotong royong is the Indonesian and Malay practice of mutual aid, in which neighbours work together on tasks a household cannot do alone.
It covers cleaning the village, building a mosque or hall, preparing a wedding or funeral, and repairing irrigation or roads.
The work is not paid and is usually not recorded; participation is a social duty, and absence is noticed.
The idea is officially promoted in Indonesia as a national value of cooperation, and it appears in government slogans and school textbooks.
In cities, gotong royong survives in neighbourhood associations, clean-up days and disaster relief, though commuting and apartment living have changed it.
exampleEn: When a neighbour dies, families in the lane coordinate cooking, seating, parking and cleaning, and nobody is asked to pay for the labour.
qualificationEn: The practice varies by region and has been romanticised as a national ideal; urban life, migration and reliance on paid services have weakened it, and it can exclude newcomers.

titleEn: Mamak stalls: Malaysia's twenty-four-hour social kitchens
facts: Mamak stalls are roadside food stalls run mostly by Tamil Muslims, found across Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore.
They serve roti canai, teh tarik, mee goreng and nasi kandar around the clock, and their open-air tables are open to men, women and families alike.
The stall works as a social space: people linger over tea, watch football, discuss politics and eat at any hour.
Mamak food is Indian-Muslim cooking adapted to local tastes, and its vocabulary mixes Tamil, Malay, English and Hokkien terms.
Neighbourhoods often take their mamak stalls' side in licensing disputes, which shows how deeply the format is embedded in urban life.
exampleEn: At 1 a.m. after a night shift a driver sits at a plastic table, orders roti canai and teh tarik, and watches a crowd of students and taxi drivers do the same.
qualificationEn: Most stalls are small businesses with uncertain licensing, and not every neighbourhood welcomes them; the Mamak identity is itself a mixed South Asian-Malay category.

titleEn: Singlish: the creole that Singapore officially discourages
facts: Singlish is the colloquial English of Singapore, shaped by Hokkien, Malay, Tamil and other languages, with distinctive particles such as lah, leh, mah and sia.
It is used informally between Singaporeans and marked by different sentence order (for example You eat already?) and abbreviated words.
The government's Speak Good English Movement has discouraged Singlish in schools and offices, arguing it damages international communication.
At the same time Singlish is a marker of national identity, used in comedies and by characters in local films and television.
The particles do real grammatical work: Can lah means roughly yes, of course, while Can or not? asks whether something is possible.
exampleEn: A waiter asks a table You all want same order?; a friend replies Can lah, sama sama, and everyone switches back to standard English in the office later.
qualificationEn: Singlish is not one fixed dialect - its features vary by ethnicity, age and class - and most Singaporeans code-switch between it and standard English rather than using one only.

expression.glossEn: yes, of course - lah marks emphasis and camaraderie

titleEn: Kiasu: the fear of losing out that Singapore jokes about
facts: Kiasu comes from Hokkien and means afraid to lose, describing the urge to grab scarce goods or advantage before someone else does.
It appears in queueing, buffets, sales, school enrolment and parking spots, and is often invoked with self-mockery.
A closely related term, kiasu-ism, is used in social commentary to describe the competitive habits of Singapore's middle class.
National campaigns, merchandise, films and comedy sketches have turned kiasu into a recognisable brand of local humour.
Critics note that the label can flatten real anxieties of an unequal city, and some Singaporeans refuse to see themselves in it.
exampleEn: When a hotel buffet opens, guests carry plates to the counter before the announcement; a family jokes about being very kiasu but still joins the queue.
qualificationEn: Kiasu is a stereotype of a diaspora-origin Hokkien term rather than a fixed personality trait; not everyone behaves this way, and competitiveness is also shaped by cost of living and education pressure.

titleEn: Javanese speech levels: the same sentence in three registers
facts: Javanese has a system of speech levels: ngoko (informal, used with peers and inferiors), madya (middle) and krama (refined, used with elders and strangers).
Vocabulary and syntax change with the register: to eat is mangan in ngoko and dhahar in krama, and a single conversation can switch levels.
Choosing the wrong level can be insulting, and children learn the system through correction by adults and in the classroom.
Krama is associated with etiquette and refinement, and it is used in formal letters, ceremonies and wayang performance.
Urban Javanese speakers increasingly mix levels with Indonesian, and many young people in cities use ngoko in most of daily life.
exampleEn: A Javanese student speaks ngoko with friends, then shifts to krama for a teacher's greeting, and later to refined krama for the respected grandfather at home.
qualificationEn: The system is not uniform across the Javanese-speaking world, and dialect variation, Indonesian dominance and generational change mean that many speakers control only part of it.

expression.glossEn: thank you - in the polite krama register

titleEn: Mudik: the homecoming that empties the cities
facts: Mudik is the Indonesian practice of returning to one's home town or village at Lebaran, the end of the Ramadan fast.
The trip can be short or enormously long; millions travel by motorbike, bus, train, ferry and car, and operators add extra services.
Returning is a social obligation: family celebrations, new clothes and asking forgiveness from parents and neighbours happen in the home village.
The government coordinates travel with police escorts and fare controls, and traffic accidents - especially for motorbike convoys - are a recurring concern.
Mudik is also a homecoming economy: money sent home and spent in villages, and a temporary reunion of children and grandparents who live apart.
exampleEn: A factory worker in Jakarta rides a motorbike with his wife and child for 14 hours through a police-escorted convoy, carrying a bag of gifts to his parents' house.
qualificationEn: Not everyone can afford to travel home, and the pandemic years disrupted the pattern; the scale and media attention vary by year, and the returning child's obligations differ by family.

titleEn: Kampong Ayer: a water village in the middle of Brunei's capital
facts: Kampong Ayer is a water village of stilt houses on the Brunei River, directly opposite the capital Bandar Seri Begawan, home to tens of thousands of people at its peak.
Houses are connected by plank walkways, and residents travel by boat or water taxi; schools, clinics and mosques have been built on the water.
