The settlement is a centuries-old trading village, and it gave its name to the Venice of the East nickname used by early travellers.
After the Second World War many residents moved to land, but the water village remains populated and is promoted as a heritage site.
Life on the water is not nostalgia only: maintenance of stilt houses and fire safety are constant practical concerns.
exampleEn: A child walks to school along a plankway from a stilt house, crosses a footbridge, and takes a water taxi to an after-school class on the riverbank.
qualificationEn: The village is smaller and more modern than its historic image, with piped water and electricity; not all residents live there by choice, and repeated resettlement policies have shaped it.

titleEn: Tetun: Timor-Leste's everyday language between Portuguese and Malay
facts: Tetun is the most widely spoken language of Timor-Leste and one of its two official languages, alongside Portuguese.
It exists in two main registers: Tetun Dili, the urban mix of Tetun, Portuguese and Malay used in daily life, and Tetun Terik, a more conservative rural variety.
Portuguese supplies administration and education vocabulary, while Indonesian and English dominate business and technology terms.
Under Indonesian rule the language was suppressed in schools, and after independence in 2002 it became a symbol of national identity.
The constitution also recognises a set of working languages, and most Timorese speak several languages across home, school and government.
exampleEn: A school in Dili begins with a greeting in Tetun, the lesson uses Portuguese textbooks, and the children joke in the Tetun-Malay mix of the playground.
qualificationEn: Language competence and use differ sharply between town and country and by generation; Portuguese remains a barrier for many, and decisions about language in education are contested.

expression.glossEn: good morning - from Portuguese bom dia

titleEn: Nowruz: the spring new year that crosses borders
facts: Nowruz marks the spring equinox and the new year in Persian and many Central Asian traditions; it is celebrated around 20-21 March across Iran, Afghanistan, Central Asia and the Caucasus.
Preparations start weeks earlier with spring cleaning, new clothes and the growing of wheat sprouts; families set a festive table with symbolic foods.
In Central Asia the scale and style vary: Kazakh and Kyrgyz families cook special dishes, Uzbek neighbours visit in turn, and Afghan households keep the haft-mewa table.
UNESCO added Nowruz to its intangible heritage list in 2009, citing its role in strengthening community ties and cultural continuity.
Under Soviet rule the holiday was discouraged in Central Asia, and it revived after 1991 as a public holiday and national symbol.
exampleEn: In Almaty a family cleans the house, cooks nauryz kozhe with seven ingredients and visits elders; in Dushanbe neighbours exchange plates of sumalak cooked overnight.
qualificationEn: Nowruz is not a single tradition: names, foods and rituals vary by country, language and religion, and not all Central Asians are equally observant.

titleEn: Buzkashi: the mounted game played at a full gallop
facts: Buzkashi is a horse-mounted game in which two teams of riders compete to carry a headless goat or calf carcass to a target circle.
The game is played mainly in Afghanistan, where it is the national sport, and in parts of Central Asia under names such as kokpar.
Riders train for years and use special saddles; the field is large and there are few formal rules, with referees enforcing custom.
Matches can last hours and sometimes injure riders and horses, and disputes over the carcass are common.
Protective helmets and boots have appeared in official tournaments, while village games keep older equipment and rough play.
exampleEn: At a wedding celebration on the steppe riders circle the carcass, a rider breaks away, and the crowd gallops after him toward the white circle on the ground.
qualificationEn: Rules, names and animal-welfare standards differ significantly between Afghan buzkashi and Kazakh or Kyrgyz kokpar, and official tournaments are unlike local games.

titleEn: Kazakhstan's alphabet: three scripts in a century
facts: Kazakh has been written in Arabic script, then Latin, then Cyrillic, and now moves back to Latin: each change was a state project rather than a gradual evolution.
Cyrillic was adopted in 1940 under Soviet rule, and Russian remains an official language of interethnic communication and the language of many urban schools.
A 2017 decree set a Latin alphabet and a target of 2025 for official use; implementation has been repeatedly delayed and the letter set revised.
The change affects education, publishing, maps and databases, and older generations learned a different spelling of every word.
Most Kazakhstanis are bilingual in Kazakh and Russian, and language policy is a sensitive issue for Russian-speaking communities.
exampleEn: A school textbook shows the same Kazakh sentence in Cyrillic and Latin, and a grandmother who learned Arabic script as a child asks her granddaughter to read the new signs at the airport.
qualificationEn: The reform's timetable has slipped, and daily practice varies between north and south Kazakhstan; Russian remains dominant in many cities, and not all Kazakhs support the Latin shift.

expression.glossEn: hello - the polite form used with elders and strangers

titleEn: Aitys: the song duel where poets improvise insults and praise
facts: Aitys is a contest of improvised poetry and song between two akyns (bards), accompanied by the dombra, in Kazakh and Kyrgyz tradition.
The duellists take turns composing verses on a chosen theme - praising a person, mocking a rival, arguing about love or social change.
Performances mix humour, wisdom and quick repartee; the audience judges the winner by its reaction.
UNESCO listed Aitys as intangible cultural heritage in 2015, describing it as a living expression of improvisational skill and community values.
State competitions and television contests keep the genre visible, and young akyns now perform in Kazakh, Russian and mixed registers.
exampleEn: Two akyns face each other at a festival yurt, pluck the dombra and trade verses about a stingy host; the audience laughs and shouts, and the loser jokes about the prize.
qualificationEn: The genre's content and audience vary between Kazakh and Kyrgyz traditions and between rural festivals and televised contests, and the improvised texts rarely survive in written form.

titleEn: Manas: an epic recited across a thousand years
facts: The Epic of Manas tells the story of a Kyrgyz warrior and his descendants; it is one of the world's longest epics, with versions running to hundreds of thousands of lines.
It is traditionally performed by manaschi, reciters who learn the text orally and may perform for hours in a heightened, chant-like delivery.
The epic combines history, myth and genealogy, and it was used in the twentieth century to shape Kyrgyz national identity.
UNESCO listed the Kyrgyz epic trilogy - Manas, Semetey and Seitek - as intangible heritage in 2013.
Manaschi training continues in schools and festivals, and the epic has been adapted into opera, film and tourism performances.
exampleEn: At a summer festival in the mountains a manaschi sits before a crowd, closes his eyes and recites a battle passage for an hour, while listeners nod at familiar lines.
qualificationEn: There is no single authorised text: versions differ by reciter and region, and Soviet-era editing shaped parts of the printed tradition.

titleEn: Jailoo: the summer migration to the high pasture
facts: Jailoo are the summer pastures of Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan where herders move with their animals from spring to autumn, living in yurts.
The migration follows snowmelt and grass: families move up in late spring and return before winter, sometimes over several stages.
Jailoo life involves milking, processing dairy products, shearing and socialising with neighbouring camps; it is also when many weddings and horse games are held.
Community-based tourism has brought visitors to some pastures, giving herders income but also changing routines.
Climate change, pasture degradation and young people leaving for cities are pressuring the system, and some families now keep animals without moving.
exampleEn: In June a family loads a yurt and kitchen onto horses and a truck, moves to a pasture at 2,500 metres, and spends the summer milking mares and making kumis beside other camps.
qualificationEn: The practice is not universal in Kyrgyzstan: many herders keep animals near villages, and the romantic image of nomadic life is often used in tourism marketing.

titleEn: Kumis: the fermented mare's milk that turns a pasture into a table
facts: Kumis is a mildly alcoholic drink made from fermented mare's milk, traditionally produced in Central Asia and Mongolia during the summer pasture season.
Mares are milked several times a day, and the milk is churned in a leather or wooden vessel and left to ferment with a starter culture.
The drink is offered to guests as a sign of hospitality, and its taste and strength vary by season and producer.
Kumis has long been valued for perceived health benefits, and sanatoria in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan once prescribed it for tuberculosis and digestion.
The drink is tied to the herding calendar: it appears when mares foal in spring and disappears when the animals return to winter quarters.
exampleEn: A visitor to a jailoo is handed a bowl of kumis at the yurt door, and after the third bowl the host begins to speak about the family's horses.
qualificationEn: Production is small-scale and seasonal, and the taste varies widely; commercial kumis is available, but traditional raw kumis is not to everyone's taste and can carry hygiene risks.

titleEn: Mahalla: the neighbourhood that governs itself
facts: A mahalla is a traditional neighbourhood community in Uzbekistan and other parts of Central Asia, centred on a mosque, tea house and communal spaces.
Residents cooperate on weddings, funerals, clean-ups and charity, and a council of elders mediates disputes.
In Uzbekistan the mahalla is also an official administrative unit, with a chairperson and a charter, and it handles social support and registration tasks.
The state uses the mahalla to deliver welfare and to monitor families, which gives it both social authority and political function.
Mahalla networks survive urbanisation and are important for migrants' families, who rely on neighbours while members work abroad.
exampleEn: When a family in Tashkent arranges a wedding, mahalla volunteers set up tables in the courtyard, coordinate cooking and collect contributions from neighbours.
qualificationEn: Mahalla organisation and state involvement differ by country and city, and rural and urban mahallas have different functions; the institution is not uniform across Central Asia.

titleEn: Osh: the plov that men cook for a crowd
facts: Osh, or plov, is a rice dish of mutton, carrots, onions and spices cooked in a large kazan (cauldron); it is the centrepiece of Uzbek hospitality.
Cooking is often done by men in the courtyard for weddings, funerals and neighbourhood events, and the recipe is a source of regional pride.
Each region has a style: Samarkand plov layers ingredients differently from Tashkent, and Bukhara uses its own spice mix.
A master cook (oshpaz) can feed hundreds from a single fire, and the order of adding rice and water is tightly controlled.
Plov is also a weekday street food sold from steaming cauldrons, and in Kazakhstan it is called palau.
exampleEn: At dawn before a wedding three men lower mutton into a huge kazan, add yellow carrots and rice, and by noon serve hundreds of guests from the same pot.
qualificationEn: Recipes and rituals differ by region and family, and the men-cooking image is a social ideal rather than an absolute rule; everyday versions are simpler and cheaper.
